findings.headline: Council is divesting from its investment portfolio and incurring £1.878m in legal costs to do so.
findings.detail: The Treasury Equalisation Reserve is being drawn down by £1.878m from an opening balance of £6.537m, with this entire drawdown attributed to legal costs of divesting the council's investments. The paper does not explain why the council is exiting its investment portfolio. This represents a material decision to liquidate investments, incurring significant professional fees.
findings.matters: Material investment divestment could indicate either a strategic treasury repositioning or liquidity pressures requiring asset liquidation. For a lender evaluating the council's financial resilience and treasury capacity, this shift warrants investigation into whether it reflects deliberate strategy or financial constraint.
findings.figures: £1.878m drawn from £6.537m opening balance for divestment legal costs; forecast balance £4.659m.
findings.quote: Funding for Legal costs associated with Divestment of the Council's investments

findings.headline: Adult Social Care reserves being heavily drawn down (£9.578m), including a new demographic pressure reserve created in December 2024 that is now entirely exhausted.
findings.detail: The council created an Adult Social Care reserve in December 2024 to fund 'ASC/CS demographic pressures' with an opening balance of £1.500m. This entire reserve is being drawn down in 2026-27. Additionally, the Adult Social Care & Health section is drawing down £8.078m from other established ASC reserves: Better Care Fund (£5.772m), Market Sustainability Funding (£0.693m), ASC - Health integration funding (£1.204m), Adults safeguarding reserve (£0.400m), and ASC grants (£0.009m). This substantial drawdown suggests demographic cost pressures are materialising faster than anticipated.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is a major service facing demographic pressures from an ageing population. The rapid exhaustion of a reserve created specifically for these pressures just months after establishment signals that ASC cost growth is acute and may force the council to increase levies, reduce services, or seek additional borrowing.
findings.figures: ASC demographic reserve created Dec 2024 with £1.500m: entirely drawn down. Better Care Fund £5.772m drawn; Market Sustainability £0.693m; ASC-Health integration £1.204m; Adults safeguarding £0.400m. Total ASC drawdown £9.578m from starting balance of £17.205m.
findings.quote: New Reserve created for ASC/CS demographic pressures as agreed at December 2024 Cabinet

findings.headline: Government grant funding projected 26% below allocation, with £14.5m shortfall
findings.detail: Government grants budgeted at £55.3m but projected to deliver only £40.8m. This large shortfall suggests either project approval delays, scheme complexity, or eligibility issues preventing the council from accessing grant funding it has budgeted.
findings.matters: A lender funding council infrastructure needs to understand whether the council can unlock promised public grant funding; a 26% shortfall on grants redirects funding pressure onto borrowing
findings.figures: Revised budget 55,310k, projected outturn 40,812k, variance -14,498k

findings.headline: Capital programme delivering only 80% of planned expenditure, with £15m variance across 75-council set
findings.detail: Total general fund capital spend projected at £60.3m against revised budget of £75.3m represents a 20% shortfall. This is material slippage that suggests either over-optimistic planning or systematic delivery constraints.
findings.matters: Persistent capital underspend raises questions about the council's realistic borrowing capacity and delivery roadmap; a lender needs to know whether the council can execute the capital plans it is borrowing for
findings.figures: Revised budget 75,344k, projected outturn 60,320k, variance -15,024k (20% underspend)
findings.quote: Total General Fund Capital Expenditure 33,440 41,122 782 75,344 60,320 -15,024

findings.headline: Two major regeneration schemes severely underdelivering, accounting for most of the capital programme shortfall
findings.detail: Grays Riverfront (GTF Project 3) is projected to spend only £727k of its £6.4m budget, and Grays Beach Park (GTF Project 4) only £425k of £8.4m. Together these leisure and regeneration schemes represent £13.6m of the total £15m capital programme underspend.
findings.matters: Large-scale project failures signal management and delivery capacity issues, with immediate implications for refinancing risk and future capital ambitions the council can realistically execute
findings.figures: Grays Riverfront: budget 6,379k, projected outturn 727k, variance -5,652k; Grays Beach Park: budget 8,419k, projected outturn 425k, variance -7,994k
findings.quote: GTF Project 3 - Grays Riverfront 6,379 0 0 6,379 727 -5,652; GTF Project 4 - Grays Beach Park & Kilverts Field - Leisure Destination 8,419 0 0 8,419 425 -7,994

findings.headline: Blackshots Housing Development demolition project delayed to January 2027, pausing a key strategic regeneration priority
findings.detail: The demolition of Blackshots high-rise blocks, described as 'a key element of the Council's estate regeneration plans', has been reprofiled. The wider redevelopment was postponed and demolition is now expected to commence in January 2027 and complete by January 2028, pushing back the initial timetable significantly.
findings.matters: Delays to major strategic housing regeneration schemes indicate project delivery constraints and limited capital resources, affecting the council's ability to execute regeneration priorities.
findings.figures: £1.400m slippage on Blackshots scheme; demolition now scheduled January 2027–January 2028
findings.quote: demolition works are expected to commence in January 2027, with completion anticipated by January 2028

findings.headline: HRA capital programme is 40% underspent with £13.4m of schemes cut beyond slippage delays
findings.detail: The capital programme is projected to spend only £29.224m against a revised budget of £48.386m. Of the £19.162m underspend, £7.353m is slippage (delayed spend), but £13.422m represents schemes 'that will not spend to budget and where funding is being released', indicating material permanent reductions to planned activity.
findings.matters: A 40% underspend and material cuts to the capital programme indicate either serious delivery challenges or affordability-driven reductions affecting the council's ability to invest and maintain housing stock.
findings.figures: £19.162m underspend (40% of £48.386m budget); £7.353m slippage; £13.422m scheme reductions
findings.quote: The HRA Capital Programme projected spend for the year is underspent by £19.162m (40%) against a revised budget of £48.386m: £7.353m of that is down to slippage; and £13.422m relating to schemes that will not spend to budget and where funding is being released

findings.headline: £3.64m of Local Authority Housing Fund grant funding is being returned to MHCLG as the council cannot utilise it
findings.detail: The council is returning £3.64m of government housing grant funding originally allocated for LAHF schemes. The document attributes this to 'the current affordability position of the HRA capital programme', indicating the council cannot deliver or afford the intended schemes despite grant availability.
findings.matters: Inability to deploy government housing grant signals either delivery constraints or affordability issues that limit the council's capacity to invest and improve housing stock.
findings.figures: £3.640m of LAHF grant funding being returned; Government Grants reduced from £6.459m budget to £1.047m projected spend
findings.quote: the Local Authority Housing Fund (LAHF) scheme is no longer expected to utilise the full level of grant funding originally allocated. In light of the revised delivery assumptions and the current affordability position of the HRA capital programme

findings.headline: Transforming Homes capital programme scaled back because schemes are unaffordable within available HRA resources
findings.detail: The council has explicitly reduced the Transforming Homes programme because it cannot afford to deliver it within current HRA financing. The document states schemes previously allocated 'is no longer considered affordable or deliverable' and are being removed from the capital programme entirely. This removes £9.633m of planned activity.
findings.matters: HRA affordability pressure that forces cuts to major programmes signals potential wider financial stress affecting the council's creditworthiness and long-term resilience.
findings.figures: £9.633m removed from Transforming Homes; total capital programme 40% underspent (£19.162m variance)
findings.quote: funding previously allocated in excess of the revised delivery requirements is no longer considered affordable or deliverable and will therefore be removed from the capital programme

findings.headline: EHCP assessments backlog deepening with only 49% of assessments completed within statutory 20-week timescale against 70% target, driven by 40% surge in requests

findings.matters: Growing special educational needs demand signals increasing long-term support obligations; delays in assessment trigger statutory duties and potential liability, and require unbudgeted additional staffing

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2025/26 Q4 and End of Year Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs remain elevated at £2,912 per week, 13% above target, driven by increasing complexity of cases
findings.detail: The average weekly cost of external placements is £2,912 in Q4, compared to the target of £2,583 and £2,500 in the previous year. The council attributes this to sustained increases in the needs and complexity of children in care, requiring higher-cost provision.
findings.matters: This is a growing structural cost pressure in a demand-led service that exceeds budget assumptions; continued growth could force further budget reallocation or use of reserves
findings.figures: £2,912 actual vs £2,583 target; £2,500 previous year
findings.quote: The overall needs of children in Thurrock's care continue to increase, resulting in a sustained requirement for higher-cost care packages. This pressure is reflected in the Q4 average placement cost, which has remained high at £2,912, compared with £2,500 in the previous year, demonstrating the ongoing financial impact of increasing complexity.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - 2025/26 Q4 and End of Year Corporate Performance Report
findings.headline: Asset divestment plan underperforming by £4.373m with £40m of major transactions reprofiled to future years
findings.detail: The council budgeted £6.175m in asset sales proceeds but delivered only £1.752m. The shortfall includes non-realisation of proceeds from Safe as Houses, PWE, TEO and the Shard investment. Additionally, significant transactions totalling an estimated £40m have been moved from 2025/26 to later years.
findings.matters: Asset receipts fund capital programmes and contribute to general liquidity; failure to realise planned receipts constrains the capital programme and may force reliance on borrowing instead
findings.figures: £1.752m actual vs £6.175m budget; £4.373m shortfall; £40m reprofiled

findings.headline: Council explicitly states its financial position remains a significant concern
findings.detail: Despite progress being made, the council identifies its financial position as a significant concern in the executive summary. This statement is made after a year in which the council achieved 95.62% of planned savings and 112% of asset disposal targets.
findings.matters: An explicit statement of unresolved financial concern from the council itself is a material risk indicator for lenders and requires immediate clarity on what specific issues remain unaddressed.
findings.figures: 95.62% of planned savings made for 2025/26; 112% of asset disposals target
findings.quote: Whilst progress is being made, the financial position of the council remains a significant concern.

findings.headline: Commercial property rental income is forecast below budget despite property savings being marked 'On Track'.
findings.detail: PLA/13/2026 (Ongoing rent reviews, £468k target) forecasts £0 delivery due to commercial property vacancies. Separately, PLA/10/2026 (Commercial Waste Income, £143.4k target) shows the key delivery post 'is yet to be recruited to' and trade waste income is 'forecast to under-recover by £234k', with £0 Q1 forecast.
findings.matters: Property-derived income is inherently volatile and sensitive to market conditions. Delayed recruitment and vacant units suggest commercial property management challenges that may persist, reducing budget flexibility.
findings.figures: Commercial property rental income forecast below budget; Commercial Waste: £234k under-recovery; £143,428 target with £0 Q1 forecast
findings.quote: overall rental income is forecast to be below budget due to vacancies within the commercial property portfolio. Work is ongoing to let the vacant units and improve the overall income position.

findings.detail: Place-based savings of £1.67m depend on Clean & Green and Housing restructure. The tracker acknowledges: 'significant expenditure on agency staff earlier in the year has resulted in a forecast overspend on employee budgets across parts of the service.' Similar restructuring risks exist in pan-organisation (Business Admin Review: only £393k of £500k delivered).
findings.matters: Reorganisation costs are already materialising while savings remain uncertain. If restructures slip or fail, the agency overspend becomes permanent and savings never arrive, creating a dual impact on year-end outturn.
findings.figures: Agency overspend across place services (unquantified); £107k of £500k Business Admin saving still undelivered

There is a risk against the delivery of the remainder.'
findings.matters: Third-party spend cuts require active procurement action. The absence of a plan for 97% of this saving at Q1 indicates either unrealistic targets or procurement capacity issues, suggesting budget credibility problems.

The recurring comment states initiatives remain unfinalised, indicating these are not delayed but fundamentally not planned.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a council's largest and fastest-growing service. Complete failure of £3.97m in ASC savings raises questions about cost control, demand management, and whether reserves will be drawn to cover this overspend.

findings.quote: ASCH/04/2026 Adult Social Care Budget Review £950,000 £0 Unachievable/Off-Track Initiatives to realise savings yet to be finalised.

findings.headline: £6.7m shortfall between planned and Q1-forecast savings (45% of £14.88m target unachieved).
findings.detail: The council planned £14,877,445 in savings for 2026/27 but Q1 forecasts only £8,163,661 delivery. Adult social care accounts for £3.2m of the gap alone, with pan-organisation and place services also significantly underperforming. Multiple large initiatives remain 'Unachievable/Off-Track' with savings plans still being finalised.
findings.matters: A £6.7m delivery gap at Q1 suggests the council's 2026/27 budget—if dependent on these savings—will not be balanced without reserves drawdown, additional cuts, or unplanned borrowing. This indicates structural budget risk.
findings.figures: Total target £14,877,445 vs Q1 forecast £8,163,661; shortfall £6,713,784
findings.quote: Key headings show: Total £14,877,445 vs £8,163,661 forecast at Q1

findings.headline: Place savings at risk totalling £557k (19% of £2.99m target) at Q1
findings.detail: Three waste-related savings are at risk: Behavioural Change Programme (£88k), Paint Reuse Scheme (£51.6k), and Commercial Waste Income (£143.4k). These represent 19% of the Place directorate's £2.99m savings programme. No commentary is provided on why these are slipping or when they will be recovered.
findings.matters: Waste-related savings slipping by Q1 suggests either demand (usage not dropping as planned) or income (commercial customers not responding to price increases as expected). This is material to Place's year-end position and signals risk of further slippage.
findings.figures: £557k at risk out of £2.99m target, Behavioural Change £88k, Paint Reuse £51.6k, Commercial Waste £143.4k
findings.quote: Of the £2.990m of savings due to be delivered in 2026/27, £0.240m have been delivered, £2.193m are on track and £0.557m are at risk.

findings.headline: Revenues and Benefits postage cost pressure of £138k driven by rising charges against static budget
findings.detail: A £138k pressure has been identified in Revenues and Benefits caused by increased billing volumes and rising postal charges, against a budget that has not been uplifted for several years. A service improvement project is underway to increase direct debit take-up and reduce postal dependency, but benefits are expected only in the medium term. Cost pressure will be managed within existing resources until the project delivers.
findings.matters: A sustained cost pressure driven by inflation in a non-discretionary area (posting bills) is real and recurring. It is being managed by deferring the cost elsewhere in the budget, masking the true pressure. If the project fails, this becomes a structural overspend.
findings.figures: £138k overspend
findings.quote: An additional budget pressure of £138k has been identified within the Revenues and Benefits Service, driven by increased postage volumes, rising postal charges, and a budget that has remained static despite these cost increases.

findings.headline: HRA rental income forecast £764k below budget; council forecasting planned reduction in temporary accommodation revenue
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is forecasting a £764k adverse variance on rental income in Q1. Forecast shows planned reduction in nightly-paid temporary accommodation from 400 to 246 by March 2027, replacing it with furnished lets and targeted prevention. This is deliberate policy but creates a revenue risk if the planned shift does not materialise.
findings.matters: A £764k rental income shortfall on HRA threatens the revenue account's financial sustainability and borrowing capacity. The forecast relies on a planned service shift (nightly-paid to furnished lets) that may face implementation risk.
findings.figures: £764k adverse variance, planned reduction in nightly-paid TA from 400 to 246
findings.quote: An adverse variance of £0.764m is forecast within Rent and Income at Period 3.

findings.headline: Commissioning & Service Delivery forecast to miss £1.5m of smarter commissioning savings
findings.detail: Within Adults and Public Health, the commissioning savings programme is projected to miss its target by £1.5m. This is driving a £1.459m service variance and is a core part of the directorate's plan to balance its position by year-end. Failure to deliver this saving will leave a structural gap.
findings.matters: A savings programme that is core to a directorate's recovery plan failing at Q1 suggests either the plan is unrealistic or delivery capacity is insufficient. This directly threatens the forecast outturn position.
findings.figures: £1.5m target, £1.459m variance
findings.quote: Commissioning & Service Delivery (Adverse £1.459m)- Primarily due to £1.5m of smarter commissioning savings forecast not to be met.

findings.headline: Corporate Services cannot achieve £220k of £473k savings target (47% unachievable)
findings.detail: The Management of Overtime saving (£120k) and Outsourcing of Print Fulfilment (£100k) are both marked unachievable. The print outsourcing has carried over from 2025/26 and has not been executed; the saving is now unlikely to happen. This represents nearly half the directorate's savings target failing to materialise.
findings.matters: A material savings programme failing to execute suggests either delivery capacity issues or a pattern of optimistic planning. By Q1, these should have been substantially underway if they were realistic annual targets.
findings.figures: £473k total target, £220k unachievable (47%), £120k Management of Overtime, £100k Print Fulfilment
findings.quote: This saving has carried over from 2025/26. The print fulfilment has currently not been outsourced, and the saving is unlikely to be achieved.

findings.headline: Business Admin Review pan-organisation saving of £500k only 79% forecast at Q1, £107k still unplanned
findings.detail: A £500k saving from a Business Admin Review has been delivered partly through deletion of vacant posts (£393k forecast), but £107k remains undelivered. Plans for delivery are still being worked on, based on role centralisation and reviews of spans and layers in newly created teams. This is a material saving that is at risk of slipping.
findings.matters: A Q1 report showing 21% of a named saving programme still lacking a delivery plan is a red flag. If this slips, the council will need to find £107k of alternative savings late in the financial year, or revise its outturn forecast downward.
findings.figures: £500k target, £393k forecast at Q1, £107k unplanned
findings.quote: The saving has been partially delivered through the deletion of vacant posts. There is approx. £107k to be delivered, and plans for the delivery of this amount are being worked on. The additional plans are based on centralisation of roles, and reviews to spans and layers of the newly created team.

findings.headline: Finance Directorate relying on £1.4m of agency staffing to cover corporate finance vacancies, despite permanent staff underspends
findings.detail: The Finance Directorate is forecasting a £675k overspend (5.5%), driven by a £525k net adverse variance in staffing costs. Corporate Finance alone shows £693k underspend on permanent staff offset by £1.4m overspend on agency staff. This pattern (hiring agency staff while underspending on permanent roles) indicates difficulty recruiting to permanent posts, forcing costly temporary cover.
findings.matters: Persistent reliance on agency staffing for core financial functions signals recruitment or retention difficulty in a critical area. It also indicates actual capacity gaps (not just vacancies that will be filled). High agency costs are non-sustainable and crowd out other spending.
findings.figures: £675k total directorate overspend, £525k staffing variance, £1.4m agency overspend, £693k permanent staff underspend
findings.quote: The variance is largely driven by agency expenditure, partially mitigated by underspends on permanent staffing budgets and recharges to HRA. This position highlights the ongoing reliance on temporary resources to maintain service delivery and operational resilience.

findings.headline: Children's Aftercare overspend of £0.386m driven by young people unable to move to independent housing
findings.detail: The service is experiencing cost pressures in supported accommodation for young people aged 18 and over who should be moving into their own properties. 14 young people remain in supported accommodation and 34 are in HMOs due to lack of available properties in the market. The council is attempting mitigation through collaboration with Housing and Commissioning to prioritise moves, but the underlying problem is supply-constrained.
findings.matters: This is a demand pressure directly tied to the local housing market, not a service control issue. It signals a structural mismatch between service need and local housing supply. If this continues, it will recur annually.
findings.figures: £0.386m overspend, 14 young people in supported accommodation, 34 in HMOs
findings.quote: The overspend is as a result of costs relating to supported accommodation. There are currently 14 young people in supported accommodation and 34 young people in HMOs. All the young people are aged 18 years or over and should be moving into their own property's but due to lack of available property's they remain in supported accommodation.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block accumulating deficit projected to reach £42.530m by end of 2028/29, driven by rising EHCP demand
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £10.307m (13%) overspend on the DSG High Needs Block in 2026/27. Underlying demand is driving this, with total EHCPs funded projected to rise from 2,791 in 2026 to 3,970 by 2029. Government support (High Needs Stability Grant) covers 90% of the eligible deficit up to 2025/26; the council will need to contribute £2.739m over three years (£0.492m in 2025/26, £1.031m in 2026/27, £1.217m in 2027/28). This is a structural problem, not a one-off adjustment.
findings.matters: A £42.5m accumulated deficit is material to council solvency and borrowing capacity. The council has no control over EHCP demand, and the statutory grant does not cover it. Future years' deficits depend on continued government support being confirmed; if it ends, the council's own resources will be consumed.
findings.figures: £10.307m Q1 overspend, £42.530m projected accumulated deficit by 2028/29, 2,791 EHCPs in 2026 rising to 3,970 by 2029, council's 3-year contribution £2.739m
findings.quote: Current forecasts show that by the end of 2028/29 financial year, the deficit is projected to be £42.530m. This reflects, both the national and local, significant increase in the number of EHCP's and the complexity of need.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care applying £9.579m of one-off reserves to cover a £4.842m in-year pressure
findings.detail: The Adults and Public Health directorate is drawing down one-off reserves to cover a Q1 pressure and is formulating a resilience plan to deliver equivalent efficiencies. The directorate's reserve balance will be depleted by this drawdown. Primary drivers are external placements (£2.719m) and commissioning savings not materialising (£1.459m). The resilience plan includes reviewing high-cost placements and income maximisation through health contributions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether services are self-sustaining or burning down cash reserves to balance. A council using one-off reserves to cover recurring pressures signals the underlying position is worse than reported.
findings.figures: £9.579m reserves drawdown, £4.842m Q1 pressure, £2.719m external placements variance, £1.459m commissioning services variance
findings.quote: The forecast outturn for Adults and Public Health as at Q1 is a pressure of £4.842m. This is after the application of one-off reserves of £9.579m. The Directorate is formulating a resilience plan, which will aim to deliver equivalent efficiencies that will lead to a broadly balanced forecast position by financial year end.

findings.headline: Finance Directorate is forecasting £0.675m overspend due to ongoing reliance on agency staffing
findings.detail: The Finance Directorate is reporting overspend driven by 'continued use of agency staff whilst permanent recruitment continues', described as 'reliance on temporary resources to maintain service delivery and operational resilience'. This is in a directorate responsible for statutory finance functions and follows 'five recruitment campaigns designed to reduce agency staff cost pressures' — yet permanent recruitment remains unsuccessful. This suggests difficulty attracting permanent talent to Thurrock finance roles.
findings.matters: Inability to recruit permanent finance staff to statutory functions creates operational risk (continuity, institutional knowledge) and signals that either pay/conditions are uncompetitive or the council's reputation as an employer in finance is weak.
findings.figures: Finance Directorate overspend £0.675m against revised budget £12.289m; agency staffing costs ongoing; five recruitment campaigns completed without sustained success
findings.quote: The Finance Directorate is forecasting an overspend of £0.675m against a net revised budget of £12.289m. This reflects the continued use of agency staff whilst permanent recruitment continues, highlighting the reliance on temporary resources to maintain service delivery and operational resilience

findings.headline: Adult Social Care income has collapsed by £3.686m year-on-year, signalling breakdown in NHS cost-sharing arrangements
findings.detail: The analysis of external placements shows income falling from £16.156m outturn to £13.834m forecast - a drop of £2.322m. Across older people, this is more severe: income fell from £2.428m to £1.308m (£1.120m loss). The council notes this requires investigation of 'Continuing Health Contributions from the NHS and contributions under S117 of the Mental Health Act', suggesting either NHS is reducing funding for joint-funded placements or the council's cost-sharing arrangements have weakened. This is flagged in the deep-dive workplan but not yet resolved.
findings.matters: Loss of income from health partners for joint-funded adult placements indicates either a policy change by health commissioners or a dispute over cost-sharing, either of which increases the council's unilateral cost exposure.
findings.figures: Total income reduction £3.686m; older people income loss £1.120m (46% of adult social care total); older people services income fell from £2.428m to £1.308m
findings.quote: The construction of the expenditure forecast needs to be validated and is helping to focus on a key number of areas such as income and recent high-cost and long-term placements... Work on income will include ensuring that Continuing Health Contributions from the NHS and contributions under S117 of the Mental Health Act are appropriate

findings.headline: Capital programme is forecast to slip by £15.624m (20%) in first quarter alone
findings.detail: Following a review of 2025/26 which saw £87.462m (73%) slippage, the Q1 2026/27 capital programme is already forecasting £15.624m underspend (20% of revised budget of £75.944m). The commissioner's report identifies this as an AMBER risk: 'Capital programme delivery remains subject to significant slippage risks, potentially delaying strategic outcomes and impacting funding and borrowing assumptions.' The review found £0.712m of prudential borrowing was released, but ongoing slippage suggests either optimistic budgeting or delivery capability issues.
findings.matters: Persistent capital programme slippage affects the timing and credibility of the council's debt reduction plan and suggests either poor forecasting or weak project management.
findings.figures: Q1 forecast underspend £15.624m; revised 2026/27 budget £75.944m; 2025/26 slippage £81.900m out of £120.250m revised budget (73%); funding released £0.712m
findings.quote: The General Fund Capital Programme is forecast to underspend by £15.624m (20%) against a revised budget of £75.944m due to slippage

findings.headline: Council budget is fundamentally dependent on £68.908m Exceptional Financial Support via Capitalisation Direction
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget of £267.290m can only be set as legally balanced by assuming £68.908m of Exceptional Financial Support (capitalisation direction), comprising £63.080m for treasury costs and £5.9m for operational deficit. This is not a one-off: the commissioner's report states 'The Council remains dependent upon Exceptional Financial Support and the Capitalisation Direction to achieve a balanced budget', flagging this as a RED risk with consequence that 'Failure to secure ongoing support or improve financial sustainability may adversely impact the Council's financial resilience.'
findings.matters: Structural reliance on government support to meet treasury costs (not one-off pressures) indicates debt sustainability concerns and governance risk if support is withdrawn or reduced.
findings.figures: Capitalisation Direction £68.908m; treasury costs budget £63.080m; operational deficit covered £5.9m; net revenue budget £267.290m
findings.quote: The Council set a net revenue budget of £267.290m for 2026/27, supported by £68.908m of Exceptional Financial Support through a Capitalisation Direction

findings.headline: Asset disposal programme is only 48% on track: £12.191m forecast against £25.320m budget
findings.detail: The asset disposal programme is critical to the council's debt reduction strategy and MTFS, but Q1 actuals of £4.025m are significantly behind the £25.320m budget. The council forecasts only £12.191m for the full year, a shortfall of £13.129m (52%). The Asset Disposals Team is undertaking a review to bring forward additional assets to recover the position, but the commissioner's report flags this as a strategic risk: 'The asset disposal programme is not currently expected to achieve its capital receipt target, which could impact the Council's debt reduction strategy.'
findings.matters: If the council cannot deliver planned capital receipts from asset sales, it will need to borrow more or reduce capital investment, both of which weaken the debt reduction trajectory that the lender base is relying on.
findings.figures: Q1 actual receipts £4.025m; full-year forecast £12.191m; full-year budget £25.320m; shortfall £13.129m; revised disposal plan target £104.100m (down from original £116.000m)
findings.quote: Total receipts for 2026/27 are currently forecast at £12.191m against a budget of £25.320m... The Asset Disposals Team is actively undertaking a review of assets with a view to bringing forward additional assets to bring the forecast back on target

findings.headline: Council is drawing down £17.871m of earmarked reserves in-year to manage current pressures
findings.detail: The council is planning to consume £17.871m of earmarked reserves during 2026/27, described as reserves 'held to meet pressures in the current year'. This represents a significant acceleration of reserve depletion to manage in-year overspends, particularly in Adult Social Care (£9.578m of the total). The council is undertaking a comprehensive review of reserves to ensure balances remain aligned to current priorities, but findings are not due until Q2.
findings.matters: Heavy reserve drawdown in Q1 of a financial year leaves limited headroom for subsequent shocks and signals the council is using one-off resources rather than solving underlying cost pressures.
findings.figures: Reserve drawdown planned £17.871m; Adult Social Care reserves drawn £9.578m; starting earmarked reserves £74.949m; general fund balance £11.000m
findings.quote: The Council is currently forecasting the use of £17.871m of earmarked reserves during 2026/27, which are held to meet pressures in the current year

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £10.307m in-year will hit £15.309m cumulatively, with 90% government cover subject to DfE approval
findings.detail: The DSG is forecasting a £10.307m in-year overspend, driven by growth in EHCP volumes, high-cost independent and out-of-borough placements, and post-16 provision. This would increase the cumulative deficit to £15.309m. Government support through the High Needs Stability Grant is expected to cover 90% of the historic deficit, but this requires DfE approval of a SEND reform plan. The remaining 10% general fund contribution is not currently in the MTFS and not included in the forecast until DfE clarifies conditions.
findings.matters: An uncontrolled DSG deficit means the council's general fund will have to absorb the 10% gap (£1.5m+) on top of current pressures, and government support is conditional on reform delivery which is not guaranteed.
findings.figures: In-year deficit £10.307m; cumulative deficit reaching £15.309m; government grant expected to cover 90% (£13.778m); residual 10% general fund liability £1.531m
findings.quote: The DSG is forecasting an in-year deficit of £10.307m due to sustained growth in demand for SEND provision and high-cost placements. This would increase the cumulative deficit to £15.309m. Government support through the High Needs Stability Grant is expected to reduce the Council's historic DSG liability by 90%, subject to DfE approval

findings.headline: Adult Social Care external placement costs are £14.420m over budget, with income also collapsing
findings.detail: The directorate is forecasting a gross overspend of £14.420m in external placements. The underlying drivers are a £6.092m increase in expenditure (mainly from higher volumes and complexity of placements) combined with a £3.686m reduction in income from the prior year, suggesting both demand growth and reduced recovery from health and mental health partners. After applying £9.578m of one-off reserve support, the net pressure is £4.842m. A deep-dive review is underway but the council has not yet demonstrated containment.
findings.matters: Demand-led overspends in social care that outrun budget assumptions and reduce expected partner income recoveries signal structural cost pressures that cannot be solved within-year and will recur.
findings.figures: Gross overspend £14.420m; expenditure increase £6.092m; income reduction £3.686m; learning disabilities placements up to £22.448m forecast from £17.137m outturn; older people placements up to £12.188m from £8.606m
findings.quote: External placement costs and non-delivery of planned savings are contributing to a forecast gross overspend of £14.420m. With the application of one-off reserves totalling £9.578m, the net overspend is £4.842m

findings.headline: Savings programme failure threatens budget control: 43% of planned savings are unachievable or at risk
findings.detail: The council planned £14.877m of savings for 2026/27, but only £8.481m is either delivered or on track. Of the unachievable or at-risk £6.397m, £3.219m relates to Adult Social Care alone, with additional £1.001m pan-organisational Smarter Commissioning savings and £0.500m Internal Customer Programme savings also off-track. The council is holding a £4.452m unallocated savings contingency to manage shortfalls, but the scale of non-delivery represents a significant financial control issue.
findings.matters: A council unable to deliver planned savings by Q1 signals underlying operational or organisational problems, and exhausts flexibility for managing future pressures without further reserves or external support.
findings.figures: £6.397m unachievable or at risk out of £14.877m target (43%); £3.219m from Adult Social Care; £1.001m pan-organisational savings not achieved; £0.500m Internal Customer Programme not achieved
findings.quote: £6.397m is currently assessed as unachievable or at risk, representing a significant financial risk to the Council and increasing reliance on alternative mitigations

findings.headline: The revised capital programme jumps to £248.285m (71% increase), with 2026/27 rising to £124.330m, concentrating failed delivery into forward years.
findings.detail: The originally-approved three-year capital programme was £144.876m. The Q1 review re-profiles £41.122m of 2025/26 slippage into 2026/27 alone, creating a revised 2026/27 budget nearly double the original. This concentration of historically-failed delivery into a single year repeats the delivery risk that generated the commissioner concerns.
findings.matters: Doubling the 2026/27 capital programme after demonstrating inability to deliver repeats the execution risk; if slippage recurs, borrowing costs escalate and infrastructure benefits defer further.
findings.figures: Revised total £248.285m (was £144.876m); 2026/27 £124.330m (was £62.500m); slippage re-profiled £41.122m
findings.quote: The revised Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29 subject to confirmation by Council is £248.285m, the 2026/27 Capital Programme is £124.330m

findings.headline: £16.716m of externally-borrowed capital failed to spend in 2025/26 and is re-profiled forward.
findings.detail: Of the £81.900m total General Fund slippage, £16.716m was funded by external borrowing. The council is now paying interest on capital not yet deployed, concentrating these non-deliveries into the forward programme.
findings.matters: Borrowed money sitting undeployed increases net debt without productive asset growth; if delivery challenges persist, debt servicing costs rise without corresponding infrastructure benefit.
findings.figures: £16.716m external borrowing slippage of £81.900m total; re-profiled £41.122m into 2026/27
findings.quote: The following table sets out the scale of the slippage of the 2025/26 General Fund Capital Programme by funding type: External Borrowing 2025/2026 £m 16.716

findings.headline: Stanford Le Hope Station and Orchard Footbridge have slipped by £6.859m and £2.598m respectively into 2026/27.
findings.detail: These major infrastructure projects are monitored separately and have experienced substantial delays. Stanford Le Hope Station alone accounts for £6.859m of the 2025/26 slippage, indicating significant project management challenges on the council's largest single capital commitment.
findings.matters: Major project delays create financing costs (interest on borrowed funds not yet deployed) and signal execution risk for future capital deployment.
findings.figures: Stanford Le Hope Station £6.859m slippage into 2026/27; Orchard Footbridge £2.598m; A13 Widening £1.501m
findings.quote: Stanford Le Hope Station (E2920) 2025/2026 Slippage into 2026/27 6.859

findings.headline: Commissioners flagged ongoing capital delivery challenges and demand stronger governance and oversight.
findings.detail: The council underspent its revised 2025/26 General Fund capital budget by £87.462m (73%), of which £82.209m was slippage. In response to this failure, commissioners explicitly required stronger governance, stricter oversight on complex schemes, and improved stakeholder engagement to assure delivery.
findings.matters: Operating under commissioner oversight with flagged delivery failures indicates governance weaknesses affecting major infrastructure deployment and future cost control.
findings.figures: £87.462m underspend (73% of revised budget), £82.209m slippage
findings.quote: commissioners commented that the slippage against the revised capital budgets, signals ongoing challenges resulting in potential delay in infrastructure improvements. Stronger governance, stricter oversight on complex capital schemes and effective stakeholder engagement will be essential

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - EY Audit Committe Update Report
findings.headline: Reserves have been unaudited over multiple years and may contain cumulative errors; council filed legal claim against 23 councils over solar asset valuation overstatements
findings.detail: LARRIG reserves assessment concluded that cumulative unaudited transactions in reserves over multiple financial years represent increased audit risk. Separately, the council filed a claim in November 2024 against 23 councils that are members of APSE, alleging they overvalued solar assets in 2017/18, leading the council to increase investment exposure and then suffer losses.
findings.matters: Reserves are critical to assessing financial resilience; unaudited balances over multiple years mean the council may be misrepresenting available resources. The APSE claim suggests the council was relying on external advice for major investment decisions that proved unreliable.
findings.figures: Reserves unaudited since 2020/21; legal claim against 23 APSE member councils; claim relates to 2017/18 valuations
findings.quote: reserves balances may include the cumulative effect of unaudited transactions arising over multiple financial years and can therefore represent an area of increased audit risk... In November 2024, the Council filed a claim against 23 councils that are members of the Association for Public Service Excellence (APSE).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - EY Audit Committe Update Report
findings.headline: Internal audit provided only 'limited assurance' on governance, risk management and internal controls for 2023/24, with insufficient 2024/25 work to support any opinion
findings.detail: The 2023/24 internal audit opinion concluded limited assurance only on the council's risk management, internal controls and governance arrangements. In 2024/25, the internal audit team completed only 9 audits against a planned programme, with the interim Head of Internal Audit confirming this was insufficient to provide a robust annual opinion. The team faces ongoing resourcing challenges.
findings.matters: Internal audit is the first line of assurance over the council's financial controls and governance; 'limited assurance' combined with understaffing indicates weak internal control environment and increased risk of undetected errors or mismanagement.
findings.figures: 2024/25: 9 audits completed; target set at 20 audits annually
findings.quote: In 2023/24 Internal Audit concluded that based on audit engagements completed during the period, that limited assurance could be provided on the Council's risk management, internal controls and governance arrangements... the Head of Internal Audit, Counter Fraud, Risk Management, and Insurance confirmed that the volume of work completed was insufficient to enable the provision of a robust Head of Internal Audit Opinion for the 2024/25 year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - EY Audit Committe Update Report
findings.headline: Council's audit readiness is significantly behind expected trajectory and rated in the worst quartile compared to similar councils
findings.detail: EY's assessment places Thurrock in Quartile 4 (the lowest category) for audit readiness among unitary and metropolitan district councils. The report states 'it is highly unlikely that audit assurances can be rebuilt to enable an unqualified opinion by 2026/27 for Thurrock Council.' Progress is significantly behind the LARRIG (Local Audit Reset and Recovery) timetable due to incomplete prior year audits and weak working paper quality.
findings.matters: Lenders rely on audit opinions to verify council financial data; a council in the worst quartile for audit readiness with very unlikely prospect of unqualified opinions within five years signals persistent financial reporting and governance weakness.
findings.figures: Quartile 4 rating; expected trajectory completion November 2026 at earliest
findings.quote: The Council's progress is significantly behind the expected timescales set out in LARRIG 01... This means it is highly unlikely that audit assurances can be rebuilt to enable an unqualified opinion by 2026/27 for Thurrock Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - EY Audit Committe Update Report
findings.headline: Council missed statutory deadlines for publishing audited financial statements and audit queries receive responses averaging 75 days late
findings.detail: The 2023/24 financial statements were not published by the 31 May 2024 deadline (published 2 May 2025) and 2024/25 were not published by 30 June 2025 deadline (published 15 August 2025). The finance team has also been slow to respond to audit queries, with approximately 30 queries outstanding and averaging 75 days overdue.
findings.matters: Late publication and slow audit responses indicate either finance team incapacity or attempts to manage disclosures, both of which reduce transparency and lender confidence in the accuracy and timeliness of financial information.
findings.figures: 2023/24 accounts published 2 May 2025 (missed 31 May 2024 deadline); 2024/25 accounts published 15 August 2025 (missed 30 June 2025 deadline); approximately 30 audit queries averaging 75 days overdue
findings.quote: The Council did not publish its 2023/24 Financial Statements by 31 May 2024 or its 2024/25 Financial Statements by 30 June 2025, as required by the Accounts and Audit Regulations... We have issued approximately 30 audit planning queries to the finance team with an average response time of 75 days overdue.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - EY Audit Committe Update Report
findings.headline: Council debt projected to reach £1.015 billion by end of 2025/26, up from £867 million at March 2025, driven by failed commercial investment strategy
findings.detail: The financial crisis originated from a commercial investment strategy involving borrowing estimated at £1.5 billion by mid-2022 to fund asset purchases. These investments deteriorated in value, resulting in impairments and losses. The council is now managing debt of £867 million (March 2025) increasing to £1.015 billion (end 2025/26).
findings.matters: The debt trajectory and the cause (failed investments rather than revenue shortfalls) indicates structural weakness in the council's decision-making and ability to recover; debt servicing costs are embedded in the capitalisation requirement.
findings.figures: £1.5 billion borrowing for investments by mid-2022; debt £867 million at 31 March 2025; projected £1.015 billion by end 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council's financial crisis stemmed largely from the Council's commercial investment strategy, which involved significant borrowing, estimated at £1.5 billion by mid-2022, to fund asset purchases. Many of these investments deteriorated in value, resulting in increased impairments.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - EY Audit Committe Update Report
findings.headline: Council issued Section 114 notice in December 2022 with £452 million deficit and remains dependent on £691 million in exceptional government support over seven years
findings.detail: The council could not set a balanced budget and received exceptional financial support of £130m (2022-23), £184m (2023-24), £96m (2024-25) and £72m (2025-26). Over seven years to 2028/29, total capitalisation directions are estimated at £691 million. The Section 114 notice expired March 2024 but the council remains under close government monitoring.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether the council can return to financial sustainability or remains permanently dependent on government bailouts; the capital financing structure is unusual and government-dependent.
findings.figures: £452 million deficit for 2023/24; capitalisation directions: £130m, £184m, £96m, £72m; total seven-year requirement £691 million
findings.quote: The Council issued a Section 114 Notice in December 2022 after concluding it could not set a balanced budget for 2022/23 and 2023/24... the Council's provisional deficit of approximately £452 million against a £153 million budget for 2023/24.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - EY Audit Committe Update Report
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinions on three consecutive years of financial statements due to unresolved prior audits
findings.detail: EY cannot issue audit opinions on 2023/24, 2024/25, or 2025/26 accounts because predecessor auditor BDO's work on 2020/21, 2021/22 and 2022/23 remains outstanding, with completion not expected until November 2026. EY will therefore issue disclaimers on all three years, meaning no audit assurance exists over the council's financial position for a three-year period.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot verify the accuracy of the council's financial statements for three years, obscuring the true scale of the financial position and reserves available to service debt.
findings.figures: Disclaimer opinions anticipated for 2023/24, 2024/25, and 2025/26; prior audits not expected complete until November 2026
findings.quote: EY will issue disclaimed opinions on the Council's 2023/24 and 2024/25 financial statements. A disclaimed opinion means that the auditor has not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to form an opinion on the financial statements.

findings.headline: FOI compliance has slipped below target: 79% of FOI requests answered within statutory deadline vs 90% target
findings.detail: The council's Freedom of Information compliance has marginally fallen below the Information Commissioner's 90% target. At mid-year 2025/26, 1,034 FOI requests had been received with 79% responded to within the statutory timeframe. Additionally, 12 Subject Access Requests are significantly beyond compliance dates due to volume and complexity, with the Information Governance team working overtime. Compliance work is underway but improving has proven difficult.
findings.matters: FOI compliance failures suggest governance and resource constraints in core administrative functions. They also indicate potential data management and records control weaknesses.
findings.figures: FOI compliance: 79% (target 90%); 1,034 FOIs received; 247 SARs received at mid-year with 80% within statutory timeframe; 12 SARs significantly overdue
findings.quote: At the mid-year point  1034 FOIs had been received and 79% responded to within the statutory timeframe, and of 247 SARs received during the period 80% were responded to within the statutory time period

findings.headline: External auditors (Ernst and Young) report issues with council responsiveness and timeliness in audit engagement
findings.detail: Ernst and Young highlighted issues experienced during the 2024/25 audit, including unresponsive officers to audit requests and failure to meet informal deadlines. In response, the Chief Finance Officer has implemented changes including designating a senior responsible officer (Deputy s151) for audit liaison, setting clear timetables for audit stages, and deploying project management governance.
findings.matters: Audit relationship problems and officer responsiveness issues suggest underlying governance and control environment weaknesses. They can delay audit clearance and delay the council's own accounts being finalised, which affects financial transparency to lenders.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Ernst and Young (EY), highlighted issues they had experienced in working with the council on the 2024/25 audit during the course of this year, including the responsiveness of officers to requests for information and the meeting of informal deadlines

findings.headline: Absence of oversight and grip on Thurrock Regeneration Limited subsidiary; options appraisal for winding up underway
findings.detail: The council acknowledges there is 'an absence of oversight and grip by the Council on TRL' (Thurrock Regeneration Limited). TRL is a wholly-owned regeneration company set up in 2013 with a subsidiary, Thurrock Regeneration Homes Ltd. The council notes there is limited knowledge of the company's status and has appointed external advisors to assist with an options appraisal, including possible winding up. This represents a governance and control weakness over a material company asset/liability.
findings.matters: Weak oversight of a wholly-owned subsidiary carrying council funding and loans represents a control gap and potential contingent liability to lenders. The council's inability to describe what its own company is doing is a governance failure.
findings.figures: TRL funded by council loans and land sales; TRL has subsidiary Thurrock Regeneration Homes Ltd
findings.quote: It is recognised that there is an absence of oversight and grip by the Council on TRL and there is a piece of work being taken forward about future planning and what happens to the subsidiary company, including whether it can be wound up

findings.headline: Children's external placement costs remain high at £2,912 per week average, up from £2,500, driven by increasing complexity of need
findings.detail: The average weekly cost of external placements in Children's Social Care has risen to £2,912 (Q4 2025/26) from £2,500 in the previous year. The council states that 'the overall needs of children in Thurrock Council's care continue to increase, resulting in a sustained requirement for higher-cost care packages.' This is an uncontrollable demand pressure on the budget.
findings.matters: Rising uncontrollable demand-driven costs in a demand-led service are a material budget risk, particularly for a council already unable to balance its budget without government support. This trend suggests budget pressures will persist.
findings.quote: The overall needs of children in Thurrock Council's care continue to increase, resulting in a sustained requirement for higher‑cost care packages. This pressure is reflected in the Q4 average placement cost, which has remained high at £2,912, compared with £2,500 in the previous year

findings.headline: Local government reorganisation creates unknown debt uncertainty: combined Thurrock-Basildon debt and Essex County disaggregation unknown
findings.detail: Thurrock is being reorganised into a unitary authority with Basildon, but the combined debt position of both councils is not yet quantified. Additionally, the value of budget disaggregation from Essex County Council is unknown. The document identifies this as presenting 'several elements of anticipated financial challenge' that could destabilise the progress made to date if not properly managed.
findings.matters: Lenders to Thurrock need to understand the council's post-reorganisation debt position. Unknown combined debt and budget disaggregation are material unknowns that affect the credit risk of the reorganised authority and potentially the terms on which existing debt can be refinanced.
findings.figures: Combined debt of Thurrock and Basildon: unknown; Essex County budget disaggregation: unknown value
findings.quote: Additional work will be required to further understand and analyse the combined debt of both Thurrock and Basildon Councils alongside the unknown value of budget disaggregation from Essex County Council

findings.headline: Finance team capacity remains limited with unfilled posts constraining progress
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that 'the capacity of the finance team remains limited' and notes that progress is inhibited by systems and processes not fit for purpose. There are open posts across finance in specific areas that have proven difficult to fill on a permanent basis. This constrained capacity affects financial management quality and control embedding.
findings.matters: A finance function constrained by capacity and vacant posts is a direct risk to the council's ability to maintain financial controls, produce reliable reporting, and manage cash and borrowing.
findings.figures: None specified; noted as ongoing recruitment challenge
findings.quote: the capacity of the finance team remains limited and to a degree, progress is inhibited by some systems and processes that are still not fit for purpose

findings.headline: Capital programme shows 73% slippage, delivering only £32.8m of £120.2m planned General Fund capital spending
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme outturn shows a £87.462m underspend (73%) against a revised budget of £120.250m, with £82.209m relating to slippage into future years. The HRA capital programme shows £30.559m underspend (50%) against £60.968m budget. The Chief Finance Officer has acknowledged that capital programme delivery is weak and has established a Capital Board to improve governance, noting that effective capital management is crucial.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver 73% of planned capital spending indicates poor project management and budget forecasting. For a council seeking to manage debt, inability to execute planned capital spending raises questions about planning rigour and project governance.
findings.figures: General Fund: £87.462m underspend (73%) on £120.250m budget; £82.209m slippage to future years; HRA: £30.559m underspend (50%) on £60.968m budget
findings.quote: The General Fund Capital Programme outturn reflects an underspend of £87.462m (73%) against the revised budget of £120.250m. Of this variance, £82.209m relates to slippage into future years

findings.headline: Chief Audit Executive rates governance, risk and control as LIMITED ASSURANCE—the weakest audit opinion
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit has issued a LIMITED ASSURANCE opinion on the adequacy and effectiveness of the council's governance, risk management and control framework. This is the lowest standard audit opinion and indicates material weaknesses in controls across the organisation. The audit plan was based on 500 audit days.
findings.matters: Limited assurance indicates material control weaknesses; lenders depend on councils maintaining strong internal control environments to safeguard borrowings and manage financial risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 Internal Audit Plan: 500 audit days

findings.headline: Government intervention extended to April 2028 because council has not met best value duty
findings.detail: Intervention was originally scheduled to end September 2025, but the 6th Commissioner report concluded the council was not yet meeting its best value duty. Intervention has been extended to cover the period up to planned dissolution through local government reorganisation, now running until 30 April 2028. A stepped-down model allows recruitment of a chief executive to replace the Managing Director Commissioner.
findings.matters: Extended intervention suggests the council's improvement trajectory is slower than anticipated and best value compliance remains uncertain. This extends governance risk to lenders.

findings.headline: Council cannot balance budget without exceptional government financial support
findings.detail: Thurrock continues to require Exceptional Financial Support from government in order to set a balanced budget. This reflects ongoing structural financial difficulty despite years of intervention and improvement efforts. The council faces a Medium-Term Financial Strategy requiring £41m in savings over three years to meet the legal duty to set a balanced budget.
findings.matters: A council requiring exceptional financial support is a higher lending risk; the ability to balance budgets independently is foundational to creditworthiness.

findings.headline: Council expects three years minimum to move from disclaimed to unqualified audit opinions
findings.detail: Under National Audit Office guidance (LARRIG), a council disclaimed for consecutive years may take up to three years to obtain an unqualified opinion. The council intends to work with EY to optimise opportunities to obtain an unqualified opinion over the next 2–3 years, aligned with local government reorganisation proposals.
findings.matters: Sustained period of audit disclaimed opinions impairs the council's financial credibility and reporting quality. Extended timeline for recovery indicates deep underlying audit or governance issues.
findings.figures: 3 years expected minimum recovery period; target is unqualified opinion for 2027/28 accounts
findings.quote: Within LARRIG is an expectation that it may take 3 years for a local authority to move from disclaimed accounts to an unqualified opinion.

findings.headline: Multiple statutory backstop dates for account publication have been missed
findings.detail: The council has missed backstop deadlines for 2020/21–2022/23 (deadline 13 December 2024), 2023/24 (28 February 2025; draft published May 2025), and 2024/25 (27 February 2026). Missing a backstop date triggers a disclaimed opinion by default, regardless of account quality.
findings.matters: Systemic failure to meet statutory reporting deadlines demonstrates persistent governance and financial control weaknesses. It also means auditors cannot issue standard unqualified opinions.
findings.figures: Backstop date for 2020/21–2022/23 was 13 December 2024; 2023/24 backstop was 28 February 2025; 2024/25 backstop was 27 February 2026; 2025/26 backstop is 31 January 2027

findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinions confirmed for 2023/24 and 2024/25, anticipated for 2025/26
findings.detail: EY will issue disclaimed opinions on 2023/24 and 2024/25 financial statements, and expects to issue a disclaimer for 2025/26. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to form an opinion on the financial statements. This arises from delays caused by the 2020/21 objection and failure to meet statutory backstop deadlines.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions, rather than unqualified opinions, indicate the auditor cannot confirm the accuracy of the council's financial position. This significantly weakens external assurance over the council's accounts and reported financial position.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2023/24, 2024/25, 2025/26)
findings.quote: EY have confirmed that they will issue disclaimed opinions on the Council's 2023/24 and 2024/25 financial statements and that their expectation is that they will also issue a disclaimer of opinion in relation to 2025/26.

Investment valuation issues in 2020/21 also contributed to delays. Following counsel opinion, the council has been in discussion with BDO on how to progress.
findings.matters: An unresolved objection blocking multiple years of audits signals a governance or accounting issue serious enough that the external auditor will not move forward. This undermines financial credibility.

Whilst the paper notes positive progress in reducing reliance on agency workers in Q4 and successful permanent conversions, the council plans to continue recruiting agency staff for Local Government Reorganisation work, which is described as the most appropriate approach.
findings.matters: A £6.3m agency overspend indicates staffing volatility and cost control challenges. While the trajectory is improving, the council's decision to use agency for LGR work signals anticipated medium-term staffing uncertainty.

findings.headline: Children's external placement costs sustained at 13% above budget amid rising complexity
findings.detail: The average weekly cost of external placements for looked-after children reached £2,912 in Q4, compared to the target of £2,583—an overspend of £329 per week. The paper attributes this to structural increases in the complexity of needs requiring higher-cost care packages. This represents a material and sustained cost pressure beyond the council's direct control.
findings.matters: This is not a temporary overspend but a structural cost pressure driven by demand complexity. For a lender, sustained cost growth in a demand-led budget line signals tightening financial flexibility, particularly if future increases are expected.

findings.quote: The overall needs of children in Thurrock's care continue to increase, resulting in a sustained requirement for higher-cost care packages. This pressure is reflected in the Q4 average placement cost, which has remained high at £2,912, compared with £2,500 in the previous year, demonstrating the ongoing financial impact of increasing complexity.

findings.headline: Asset disposal plan delivering less than one-third of target and major receipts reprofiled

Beyond this, significant transactions totalling approximately £40m have been reprofiled into future financial years. The shortfall stems from non-realisation of planned receipts from specific assets including Safe as Houses, PWE, and lower proceeds than anticipated from TEO and the Shard investment.
findings.matters: Asset disposals are typically a key component of council financing plans and borrowing assumptions. A £4.4m shortfall plus £40m in delayed receipts signals cash-flow pressure and potential implications for the council's medium-term financial strategy.
findings.figures: Delivered £1.752m against budget £6.175m (28% outturn); £40m of significant transactions reprofiled to future years

findings.headline: HRA Repairs & Maintenance overspent by £1.178m due to backlog and Awaab's Law compliance costs
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account reported a breakeven position with £1.702m added to reserves, but within that, Repairs & Maintenance overspent by £1.178m. The paper cites 'a backlog of works, higher void repair costs, and additional activity to meet compliance requirements, including Awaab's Law' as drivers. Awaab's Law (relating to damp and mould in social housing) creates a new regulatory compliance obligation. While Supervision & Management underspent by £1.174m (largely from vacancies and insurance recoveries), the repairs overspend is the underlying operational pressure.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance backlogs are costly to clear and Awaab's Law creates an unfunded compliance obligation for social landlords. The HRA cannot simply avoid these costs — they are regulatory or safety-driven. This signals future HRA budget pressure and may limit flexibility to support the General Fund through HRA contributions.
findings.figures: HRA Repairs & Maintenance overspend £1.178m; driven by backlog of works, void repair costs, and Awaab's Law compliance
findings.quote: Repairs and Maintenance: The service reports an overspend of £1.178m, an increase of £0.486m from Quarter 3. This is primarily due to a backlog of works, higher void repair costs, and additional activity to meet compliance requirements, including Awaab's Law.

findings.headline: Divestment receipts fell £4.373m short of budget, with £40m of major transactions now pushed into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council budgeted £6.175m in divestment receipts for 2025/26 but received only £1.752m (71% shortfall). Key drivers: Safe as Houses contributed £0m (budget £3.0m), PWE contributed £0m (budget £0.8m), and TEO underperformed (£0.469m actual vs £1.0m budget). Critically, 'significant transactions with an estimated combined value of £40m, originally expected in late 2024/25 and reprofiled into 2025/26 will now be achieved in 2026/27'. Additionally, the forecast for total divestment receipts to 2028/29 has been reduced by £3.55m from previous assumptions due to 'updated expectations of market conditions'. The paper notes these are being used to reduce the council's Capital Financing Requirement.
findings.matters: Divestment delays and revised downward forecasts signal the council's asset disposal programme is not executing as expected and market conditions are tightening. If receipts are being counted on to reduce borrowing and capital financing costs, delays mean higher future borrowing costs and cash flow tightening. The £40m push into 2026/27 is a material refinancing risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 divestment budget £6.175m, actual £1.752m (variance £4.373m adverse); Safe as Houses £0m vs £3.0m budget; PWE £0m vs £0.8m budget; TEO £0.469m vs £1.0m budget; £40m of transactions moved from 24/25/early 2025/26 into 2026/27; forecast to 2028/29 reduced by £3.55m from prior assumptions
findings.quote: Actual receipts were £1.752m, resulting in an adverse variance of £4.373m. This is mainly due to delays in asset disposals (including Safe as Houses and PWE), lower-than-expected receipts from TEO... In addition, significant transactions with an estimated combined value of £40m, originally expected in late 2024/25 and reprofiled into 2025/26 will now be achieved in 2026/27... The forecast for total receipts to 2028/29 is £100.55m, a reduction of £3.55m from previous assumptions, reflecting updated expectations of market conditions.

findings.headline: Finance directorate relies on £1.500m of agency staffing overspend to maintain statutory functions — flagged as structural pressure requiring action
findings.detail: The Finance Directorate overspent by £0.724m in 2025/26, but the core issue is structural: Corporate Finance recorded a £1.033m overspend driven 'primarily by significant agency staffing pressures of £1.500m, reflecting the requirement to maintain statutory and operational delivery'. This overspend is only partially offset by underspends on permanent staff vacancies. The directorate's MTFS commentary (section 7.19) explicitly states: 'These issues remain ongoing and are reflected within the Medium Term Financial Strategy. Actions are required to reduce dependency on agency resources, deliver sustainable workforce solutions'. This signals the council cannot currently attract or retain permanent staff in core finance roles.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on agency staff to deliver statutory finance functions (payroll, ledger, treasury) signals either market-driven wage pressure (indicating the council is uncompetitive) or structural vacancy (indicating capacity/culture issues). Statutory finance functions cannot be outsourced or cut; the council is paying a premium to keep them staffed. This is a run-rate cost pressure.
findings.figures: Finance Directorate overspend £0.724m; Corporate Finance overspend £1.033m; agency staffing overspend within Corporate Finance £1.500m; permanent staffing underspends partially offset this but do not eliminate it
findings.quote: significant agency staffing pressures of £1.500m, reflecting the requirement to maintain statutory and operational delivery... Actions are required to reduce dependency on agency resources, deliver sustainable workforce solutions and review cost recovery and income assumptions to ensure long-term financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Children's services placement costs are rising despite numbers being below budget, indicating complexity-driven cost inflation
findings.detail: Non-DSG Children's Services reported an underspend of only £0.008m in 2025/26, but this masks significant demand pressures. Placements and Support overspent by £1.151m while the actual number of placements (259) remained below the budget assumption of 275. This means each placement is costing more: external residential placements cost £14.564m for 27 placements (budget £11.405m for 27), and supported accommodation cost £1.574m for 20 placements (budget £1.038m for 16). The paper explicitly states costs are 'increasing due to greater complexity of need and higher support packages'. Additionally, No Recourse to Public Funds (NRPF) overspent by £0.707m — a statutory pressure where the council must house homeless families with dependent children.
findings.matters: Rising unit costs per placement, even as volume stays flat or falls, signal that the council is managing higher-need cases. This is not a volume problem that can be controlled; it is a complexity problem that raises costs regardless of headcount. Both NRPF and placements are statutory or near-statutory, limiting the council's ability to control spending.
findings.figures: Placement Support/Placements overspend £1.151m; actual placements 259 vs budget 275; External Residential 27 placements cost £14.564m vs budget £11.405m (variance £3.159m); Supported Accommodation 20 placements cost £1.574m vs budget £1.038m (variance £0.536m); NRPF overspend £0.707m
findings.quote: While the number of placements (259) remains below the budget assumption (275), costs are increasing due to greater complexity of need and higher support packages. In addition, ad hoc placement costs increase, reflecting higher overall placement activity, greater complexity of need, and increased unit costs, which together drive the financial pressure.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast to reach £42.530m by 2028/29, driven by exponential EHCP demand growth
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £5.302m in 2025/26 (2.94% of the £71.976m budget), with the High Needs Block alone accounting for £6.251m of that overspend. The council's DSG Management Plan forecasts the accumulated deficit will reach £42.530m by 2028/29 if current demand trends continue. The drivers are clear: total EHCPs/places funded by High Needs Block forecast to grow from 2,791 (2025/26) to 3,970 (2028/29), while High Needs expenditure is forecast to rise from £48.055m (2025/26) to £61.854m (2028/29), against assumed DSG funding rising only to £46.717m. Though the government announced a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the deficit up to end 2025/26, Thurrock must contribute the remaining 10% (£0.492m in 2025/26, £1.031m in 2026/27, £1.217m in 2027/28).
findings.matters: A spiralling DSG deficit is not discretionary spending — it is statutory SEND provision. A £42.5m accumulated deficit by 2028/29 signals fundamental mismatch between the council's SEND offer and its funding, and the government's stability grant covers only part of the problem for only three years. This creates ongoing structural pressure on the General Fund.
findings.figures: 2025/26 DSG overspend £5.302m; High Needs Block overspend £6.251m; Accumulated DSG deficit forecast: 2026/27 £4.919m, 2027/28 £15.226m, 2028/29 £42.530m; Thurrock's 10% contribution obligation £2.739m over 2025/26–2027/28
findings.quote: Officers continue to work with the Schools Forum to consider the financial challenges arising from the significant increase in demand for EHCP's and complexity of need; alongside the sufficiency of the local offer to prevent high-cost external placements. Current forecasts show that by the end of 2028/29 financial year, the deficit is projected to be £42.530m.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care has a £3.178m structural overspend that requires permanent solution from 2027/28 onwards
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care & Health directorate overspent by £3.178m in 2025/26, driven primarily by external placement costs (£1.659m), with particular pressures in Learning Disabilities (£0.576m from young people transitioning to adult services) and Mental Health (£0.863m from demand volatility). The council explicitly states that this is a structural deficit: unless addressed, it will 're-emerge and compound the challenge in future years' and the MTFS from 2027/28 will need to incorporate 'a permanent solution, whether through demand management, service transformation, additional funding, or savings'.
findings.matters: A structural budget gap that the council acknowledges cannot be managed through one-off mitigations signals ongoing spending pressure that will require either service cuts or additional funding — material risk for a lender assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: £3.178m overspend; External placements £1.659m (Older People £0.220m, Learning Disabilities £0.576m, Mental Health £0.863m); external placement demand driven by 'increased demand, complexity of need and higher placement costs'
findings.quote: Unless the structural budget gap is addressed, this pressure will re-emerge and compound the challenge in future years. From 2027/28 onwards, the Medium-Term Financial Strategy will therefore need to incorporate a permanent solution, whether through demand management, service transformation, additional funding, or savings, to ensure that the budget is brought back into a sustainable position.

findings.matters: Asset sales provide one-time cash but erode recurring revenue base; councils using asset disposals to balance operating budgets create structural deficits as the asset base depletes

findings.detail: PLA 19 reports Selective Licensing income exceeded target by approximately £1m in 2025/26, with surplus transferred to reserves for future scheme activities. findings.headline: Finance restructure delivered savings but department is running significant agency staff overspends
findings.detail: The Corporate Finance Structure review achieved its £200k permanent savings target through staff reductions. However, the Finance department is simultaneously running 'significant overspends on agency staff'. The commentary notes savings 'are on track for full delivery by year-end' but acknowledges offsetting contingent labour costs.
findings.matters: Agency overspends offsetting restructure savings suggest either the restructure was insufficient or the department cannot operate at intended staffing levels, creating ongoing cost pressures that mask true savings delivery
